title: Where the drowned were taken
source_text: Ὑπιδόμενος δ᾿ ἑξῆς ὁ Κέλσος τάχα δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς συνιδὼν, ὅ τι δύναται λεχθῆναι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀπολογουμένων περὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ κατακλυσμῷ διαφθαρέντων, φησίν· εἰ δὲ μὴ διαφθείρει τὰ ἴδια ἔκγονα, ποῖ ποτε αὐτὰ ὑπεξάγει τοῦ κόσμου τοῦδε, (??)ν ἐποίησεν αὐτός; καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο δὲ λέγομεν ὅτι τοῦ μὲν παντὸς κόσμου, συνεστῶτος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, οὐ πάντως ὑπεξάγει τοὺς τὸν κατακλυσμὸν πεπονθότας, ἀπαλλάττει δ᾿ αὐτοὺς τῆς ἐν σαρκὶ ζωῆς καὶ ἀπολύσας τῶν σωμάτων ἀπολύει ἅμα καὶ τοῦ ἐπὶ γῆς τυγχάνειν, ἣν πολλαχοῦ τῶν γραφῶν ἔθος ὀνομάζεσθαι κόσμον. μάλιστα δ᾿ ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ἰωάννην εὐαγγελίῳ πολλάκις ἔστιν εὑρεῖν κόσμον τὸν περίγειον ὀνομαζόμενον τόπον, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν τῷ „ἦν τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν, ὃ φωτίζει πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐρχόμενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον,“ καὶ „ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ θλῖψιν ἔχετε· ἀλλὰ θαρσεῖτε, ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον.“ εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀκούει τις τοῦ ὑπεξάγει τοῦ κόσμου τοῦδε τοῦ περιγείου τόπου, οὐδὲν ἄτοπον ἀπαντᾷ τῷ λόγῳ· εἰ δὲ κόσμον τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς σύστημα ὀνομάζει τις, οὐ πάντως οἱ τὸν κατακλυσμὸν παθόντες ὑπεξάγονται ἀπὸ τοῦ οὕτως ὀνομαζομένου κόσμου. καίτοι γε εἴποι ἄν τις, νοήσας τὸ „μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα“ καὶ τὸ „τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται,“ ὅτι πρὸς τοῖς ἀοράτοις καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ὀνομαζομένοις μὴ βλεπομένοις τυγχάνων ὑπεξῆλθε τὸν κόσμον, τοῦ λόγου αὐτὸν ὑπεξάγοντος ἐντεῦθεν καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ὑπερουράνιον ἐπὶ τῇ θέᾳ τῶν καλῶν μετατιθέντος τόπον.
pass_a_gloss: Suspecting (ὑφοράω) next, Celsus, and perhaps himself perceiving (συνοράω) what can be said by those defending (ἀπολογέομαι) [the case] of those destroyed in the flood, says: ‘but if he does not destroy his own offspring, where ever (ποῖ ποτε) does he remove (ὑπεξάγω) them from this world (κόσμος) which he himself made?’ To this we say that from the whole world, composed (συνίστημι) of heaven and earth, he does not entirely remove those who suffered the flood, but he frees (ἀπαλλάττω) them from life in flesh (σάρξ), and having released (ἀπολύω) [them] from bodies (σώματα) releases [them] at the same time from being on earth, which in many places of the Scriptures it is customary to name ‘world’. Especially in the Gospel according to John one can often find the place around the earth (περίγειος τόπος) named world, as in ‘was the true light which enlightens (φωτίζω) every man coming into the world’, and ‘in the world you have affliction (θλῖψις); but take courage (θαρσέω), I have conquered (νικάω) the world’. If one hears ‘removes from this world’ as of the place around the earth, nothing absurd (ἄτοπος) meets the argument; but if one names world the system (σύστημα) of heaven and earth, those who suffered the flood are not entirely removed from the world so named. And yet one might say, having understood ‘we not looking at (σκοπέω) the things seen but the things not seen’ and ‘for his invisible things (ἀόρατα) from the creation (κτίσις) of the world are discerned (καθοράω), understood (νοέω) by the things made (ποιήματα)’, that one being among the invisible and, simply, the things named not-seen has gone out from (ὑπεξέρχομαι) the world, the Word/reason (λόγος) removing him from here and transferring (μετατίθημι) [him] to the super-heavenly (ὑπερουράνιος) place for the vision (θέα) of the beautiful things (τὰ καλά).
pass_b_english: Next Celsus, suspecting, and perhaps himself perceiving, what could be said about those destroyed in the flood by those who make the defence, says: “But if He does not destroy His own offspring, where then does He remove them to, out of this world which He Himself made?”

To this too we say that He by no means removes those who suffered the flood from the whole world, which consists of heaven and earth. But He frees them from life in the flesh, and, in releasing them from their bodies, He releases them at the same time from being on the earth, which in many places of the Scriptures is commonly called “world.” Especially in the Gospel according to John one can often find the region around the earth called “world,” as in: “That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9), and: “In the world you have affliction; but take heart, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

If, then, someone takes “He removes them out of this world” to mean this region around the earth, nothing absurd follows for the argument. But if someone calls “world” the system made of heaven and earth, those who suffered the flood are by no means removed from the world so named. And yet a person who has understood the words: “while we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are not seen” (2 Corinthians 4:18), and: “For His invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made” (Romans 1:20), might say that one who is occupied with the invisible things, the things called, in a word, “not seen,” has gone out of the world, since the Word removes him from here and moves him to the region above the heavens (Plato, Phaedrus 247c) to behold the things that are beautiful.

choices.choice: Koetschau’s text has a damaged letter before ν ἐποίησεν; read ὃν (‘which He made’), which the sense requires. οὐ πάντως (twice) is rendered ‘by no means’: Origen denies outright that the drowned leave the cosmos of heaven and earth, and then turns (καίτοι γε) to a different case, the contemplative. ‘One who is occupied with the invisible things’ renders πρὸς τοῖς ἀοράτοις … τυγχάνων. In the last sentence τοῦ λόγου could mean ‘the Word’ (Christ) or ‘reason’; rendered ‘the Word’ as Origen’s usual sense when describing the soul’s ascent, but ‘reason’ is possible. ‘The region above the heavens’ (ὑπερουράνιος τόπος) and ‘the vision of the beautiful things’ echo Plato, Phaedrus 247c. ‘Those who make the defence’ renders τῶν ἀπολογουμένων.
removed added words 'the account of' (περὶ τῶν … διαφθαρέντων means 'about those destroyed')
Celsus: 'where on earth does He take them away to' -> 'where then does He remove them to' (ποῖ ποτε; the idiom 'on earth' clashed with the earth/world argument); later echo made consistent
οὐ πάντως: 'not altogether' -> 'by no means' twice (the old wording implied a partial removal)
'the argument meets nothing absurd' -> 'nothing absurd follows for the argument' (calque)
removed added 'whole' before 'system made of heaven and earth'
'one who comes to be among the invisible things' -> 'one who is occupied with the invisible things' (πρὸς τοῖς … τυγχάνων)
checked John 1:9, John 16:33, 2 Corinthians 4:18, Romans 1:20, Plato Phaedrus 247c

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
